lesson.title: 5G NR: A Radio Interface Built for Three Different Jobs at Once
lesson.summary: 5G NR is the 3GPP air interface standard that replaced LTE's one size fits all radio with flexible numerology spanning sub 6 GHz and millimeter wave spectrum, letting one network serve everything from gigabit streaming to millisecond grade industrial control.
lesson.body:
5G NR (New Radio) is the air interface standard the 3GPP began publishing in Release 15, and it exists because the cellular network architecture that carried 4G LTE hit a ceiling no amount of tuning could push past. LTE was built around one dominant traffic pattern: a phone streaming video or browsing the web. 5G NR had to serve three very different jobs with one radio: enhanced mobile broadband for fast browsing and streaming, massive machine type communication for millions of low power sensors, and ultra reliable low latency communication for things like remote surgery and industrial robotics. Meeting all three meant rethinking the physical layer, not just adding antennas to LTE.

The feature that makes this possible is scalable numerology. LTE fixed its subcarrier spacing at 15 kHz everywhere. 5G NR lets an operator pick 15, 30, 60, 120, or 240 kHz depending on the deployment: wider spacing shortens each OFDM symbol, cutting latency and tolerating the Doppler shift and phase noise common at high frequencies, while narrower spacing favors wide coverage. This flexibility is also why 5G NR spans two frequency ranges. FR1 covers sub 6 GHz spectrum, roughly 410 MHz to 7.125 GHz, the same general territory 4G LTE already used. FR2 covers millimeter wave spectrum from 24.25 GHz to 52.6 GHz, where huge amounts of unused bandwidth sit largely idle but signals struggle to pass through a wall or even heavy rain.

5G NR can be rolled out two ways, and the difference matters more than the marketing suggests. Non standalone (NSA) mode anchors the 5G radio to an existing 4G LTE core, so a phone keeps its control connection on LTE while using 5G only for data traffic; most early launches used NSA because it reused infrastructure already in the ground. Standalone (SA) mode connects to a purpose built 5G core instead, which unlocks network slicing, the ability to carve one physical network into several virtual ones each tuned for a different job, and the sub millisecond latency that ultra reliable low latency communication actually needs.

The headline numbers attached to 5G NR, up to 20 Gbps downlink and 10 Gbps uplink under the ITU's IMT 2020 targets, are ceilings reached only with wide millimeter wave channels, massive MIMO antenna arrays, and beamforming that aims signal energy at one device instead of spraying it everywhere. Real world throughput depends heavily on proximity to a cell site and how much spectrum an operator has actually cleared for use, which is why 5G's most consistent gains often show up in latency and capacity rather than the advertised peak speed.

Because 5G NR still organizes devices into cells the same way earlier cellular network generations did, a moving device still has to hand its active session from one cell to the next without dropping it, the same handoff problem that predates 5G by decades. What changes is scale: millimeter wave cells are physically smaller, so a device crossing a busy area may need to hand off far more often, and NSA deployments add a second layer of handoff between the 5G radio and the underlying 4G LTE anchor.
